sections.heading: What is the Fast & Slow Pointers Pattern?
sections.content: Fast & Slow Pointers (also called Floyd's Tortoise and Hare) uses two pointers that move through a sequence at different speeds. The slow pointer moves one step at a time and the fast pointer moves two steps. Because of the speed difference, the pointers reveal structure such as cycles and midpoints without extra memory. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Detect a cycle in a linked list or a sequence
Find the start of a cycle or the cycle length
Find the middle of a linked list
Find the Nth node from the end
Check if a linked list is a palindrome
Problems where a value repeats and forms a loop (Happy Number, Find the Duplicate)
You cannot use a HashSet because of O(1) space limits

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Imagine two runners on a circular track. The faster runner will eventually lap the slower one, so they must meet. On a straight track the fast runner just reaches the end first. So if the two pointers ever meet, there is a cycle. If the fast pointer reaches null, there is none. When the fast pointer reaches the end of a list, the slow pointer is exactly at the middle.

Why Phase 2 Finds the Cycle Start
sections.content: Let the distance from head to the cycle start be a, and the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point be b. At the meeting, the slow pointer has walked a + b and the fast pointer has walked twice that. The extra distance walked by fast is a whole number of cycle lengths, which means walking a more steps from the meeting point lands exactly on the cycle start. So a pointer from head and a pointer from the meeting point meet at the cycle start.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Not checking fast and fast.next for null, which causes NullPointerException
Comparing node values instead of node references (use === in Kotlin)
Forgetting that the middle is the second middle on even lists with the basic template
Not using a dummy node when the head itself might be removed
Moving both pointers after the meeting in phase 2 at different speeds
Forgetting to cut the list (slow.next = null) before reversing the second half
Using !! carelessly in Kotlin without confirming the node is not null

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Fast moves two steps and slow moves one, so they meet only if there is a cycle
When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle
After the meeting point, reset one pointer to head and move both one step to find the cycle start
A gap of n between pointers finds the Nth node from the end
Any sequence where next is a function of the current value can be treated like a linked list
This pattern gives O(1) space where a HashSet would need O(n)
